questions.question: What is the starting point of integration by substitution Type 1?
options: Propose a new variable of the form $t = g(x)$.
Propose a parametrisation of the form $x = \varphi(t)$.
Differentiate both sides of an equation twice.
Replace every function by its inverse function.
questions.explanation: Type 1 begins by naming an inner expression directly: $t=g(x)$.
option_explanations: Writing $x=\varphi(t)$ is Type 2.

Type 1 substitution begins by naming an inner expression $t=g(x)$ and using its first derivative $g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\mathrm{d}t$ to change variables; differentiating twice produces $g''(x)$, which never enters the chain-rule identity $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$.
Inverse functions are not substituted universally.
